Quick Facts
Official ballot title: The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 (SB 417, Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026, Limón).
Type: Legislative referral (general obligation bond act). Placed by the legislature, not by citizen signatures.
A vote YES means: The state may borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds. This includes about $10 billion in general obligation bonds that would fund affordable housing construction, rehabilitation, and homeownership programs, repaid from the general fund, and about $1.25 billion in revenue bonds funding CalVet home loans, repaid by the veterans who borrow.
A vote NO means: The state does not authorize this borrowing. Existing state housing programs continue with whatever money remains from prior bonds and the annual budget.
Sponsor/proponent: Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón (lead Senate author) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (lead Assembly author), with Gov. Gavin Newsom, who signed the measure onto the ballot June 25, 2026.
On the ballot because: The legislature passed SB 417 by the required two-thirds vote and the governor signed it. Bond acts must go to the voters. The Senate concurred twenty-nine to two on June 25, 2026.
Full legal text: SB 417, California Legislative Information (leginfo) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office ballot analysis, Proposition 1 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 1 asks California voters for permission to borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds, with the money directed at affordable housing and veteran homeownership. It is a general obligation bond measure, which is the standard way the state borrows for long-lived investments and pays the money back over time out of the annual budget—requiring higher tax revenues or lower spending on other items.
The measure splits into two very different pieces. The larger piece is $10 billion in general obligation bonds for what it calls affordable housing programs (and what detractors call “subsidized” housing programs). That money would refill the state’s main housing accounts, most of which have spent down the funds from the last housing bond, 2018’s Proposition 1. The bill directs $5.1 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program that finances rental construction, with another $1.15 billion inside that program reserved for housing tied to homelessness and social programs aimed at homelessness. Smaller amounts go to homeownership help, farmworker housing, tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure that supports new residential building.
The smaller piece is $1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program, which offers below-market mortgages to veterans. This piece matters for how voters should read the price tag. CalVet loans are mostly repaid by the veterans who take them out, so this portion is designed to carry its own cost rather than fall on the general fund. The headline number is $11.25 billion, but the part that taxpayers repay is the $10 billion housing bond.
2. The legal language
Full text: SB 417, “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026)
Key language:
“Bonds in the total amount of ten billion dollars ($10,000,000,000), exclusive of refunding bonds issued pursuant to Section 54076, or so much thereof as is necessary as determined by the committee, are hereby authorized to be issued and sold.”
What it amends: Adds Part 16.1 (commencing with Section 54050) to Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, which houses the affordable housing programs, and Article 5ab (commencing with Section 998.750) to the Military and Veterans Code, which authorizes the CalVet loan bonds. Because a bond act is enacted by the voters, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own, though it does set the program rules that govern how the money is spent.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who authored it? Authored by Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, backed by Governor Newsom and a large roster of Democratic coauthors, along with a coalition of housing developers, labor, and veterans’ groups who would receive the subsidies. The named opposition is a small number of Republican legislators and free-market groups such as the Pacific Research Institute.The bond passed with almost no Republican support, and the Senate concurrence vote was twenty-nine to two.
What does it do? Authorization to sell $11.25 billion in bonds: roughly $10 billion in general obligation bonds for affordable rental housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure, plus $1.25 billion in revenue bonds for CalVet home loans.
Where does it apply? Statewide. The money flows through existing state housing programs administered chiefly by the Department of Housing and Community Development and the Department of Veterans Affairs.
When would it take effect? Decided on the November 3, 2026, ballot. If approved, the state would sell the bonds over several years as projects come online and repay them over roughly twenty-five years.
Why did supporters put it on the ballot? Supporters point to California’s housing affordability and homelessness crisis and argue the state needs a dedicated capital source because prior bond money is nearly gone. Their stated goals are to build and preserve “affordable” homes, expand homeownership for lower-income residents and veterans, and leverage federal and private dollars.
4. Trade-offs
A bond is first and last a borrowing and subsequent repayment decision. The Legislative Analyst estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing portion would cost the general fund roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years. That is money committed to interest and principal for a quarter century, unavailable for schools, healthcare, or anything else, and locked in regardless of the state’s budget condition in any given year. California’s independent analyst frames the real cost plainly. Paying for these programs with borrowed money rather than cash on hand costs the state about 15 percent more after adjusting for inflation. In nominal dollars the gap is larger. One outside estimate puts total repayment near $17.4 billion, of which about $7.4 billion is interest, so a large share of every repayment dollar buys interest rather than housing. Either way, the honest statement is that borrowing is not free, and the premium is the price of building now instead of later.
The case for paying that premium is not weak, and voters should weigh it fairly. Housing is a long-lived asset, and financing long-lived assets with long-term debt is a defensible match, the same logic a family uses for a mortgage. The programs the bond refills are largely spent out, so the practical alternative is not cheaper cash, it is less housing built during a severe shortage. Supporters also argue that each state dollar pulls in roughly four dollars of federal tax credits, local funds, and private capital, which means the state’s borrowing is not the whole capital stack but a match that unlocks the rest.
Voters should also consider the usefulness of government-provided and allocated so-called affordable housing. The record of massive cost overruns (hundreds of thousands of dollars for tiny homeless units) is not encouraging. Affordable housing is really taxpayer-subsidized housing. When it is allocated to people with low incomes, people have to win lotteries and then face the danger of losing their housing subsidies if they earn more money or have an opportunity to get a better job if they move. It can lock people into poverty. The state and cities already pour large amounts into so-called affordable housing directly, and this plan would force developers to create such housing in return for permission to build market-rate housing. Voters should consider if more is needed. Finally, the central source of the housing affordability crisis is the state’s and cities’ limitations on private housing construction. Creating more government-subsidized and politically allocated housing instead of simply allowing people to build houses would, arguably, only make the crisis worse.
That is the trade-off. On one side, a $500 million to $600 million annual claim on the budget for twenty-five years and an inflation-adjusted premium of about 15 percent for borrowing rather than paying cash. On the other side, potentially tens of thousands of affordable and supportive homes financed during a housing emergency, with outside money leveraged on top, but potentially more boondoggles. This bond does nothing to cut the existing red tape around building “affordable” housing. The sharper question is not whether housing is worth building. It is whether a general obligation bond, repaid by all taxpayers over a generation, to fund government provision and allocation of more housing, is the right tool, or whether the same goal should compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against everything else each year.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Refills the state’s main affordable housing accounts, most of which have drained the 2018 bond funds, so the money would sustain construction during a severe shortage.
Directs the largest share, $5.1 billion, to the Multifamily Housing Program, with $1.15 billion for supportive housing aimed at homelessness.
Matches long-term debt to a long-lived asset, the same financing logic used for other capital investments.
Reportedly leverages roughly four dollars of federal, local, and private capital for each state dollar, expanding the total built.
Expands homeownership at little direct taxpayer cost since the $1.25 billion CalVet portion is designed to be repaid by veteran borrowers, not the general fund.
Potential risks
Commits the general fund to roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years, money unavailable for other priorities regardless of the state’s fiscal condition.
Produces borrowing costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying for the same programs with cash, and a large share of nominal repayment is interest.
Arrives as California faces budget deficits, adding a fixed cost on top of existing bond debt already near $6 billion a year in debt service.
Says nothing about the permitting, land, and labor costs that drive California’s high per-unit building costs, so more money does not guarantee proportionally more units.
Accepts that the leverage and unit-count claims come largely from proponents and assumes federal credits and local matches materialize as projected.
Builds housing that by definition does not pay for itself, leading people to live where they do not want to live and trapping them away from economic opportunity. There’s a potential for great waste.
6. Open questions
What will each subsidized unit actually cost to build with this money, and how many homes will $10 billion buy at current California construction costs?
Who will get them and how?
Does bond financing add enough housing sooner to justify the inflation-adjusted premium over paying cash through the budget?
How firm is the “four dollars leveraged per state dollar” claim once federal credit availability and local matches are tested?
Given projected deficits, what other spending gives way when $500 million to $600 million a year is committed to debt service for twenty-five years?
How much of the money reaches new construction versus preservation and program overhead, and who tracks the units delivered?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A bond is a decision to build now and pay later, with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office says borrowing for these housing programs costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying cash. Before you vote, ask whether building affordable homes during this shortage is worth that premium and a $500 million to $600 million yearly claim on the budget for the next twenty-five years.
Almost every voter wants more affordable housing. But government-provided housing is not more affordable to the state as a whole. It is only affordable to the select few recipients because taxpayers pay for it. The real question is the tool. Should this spending be locked in as bond debt that all taxpayers repay over a generation, or should it compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against schools, healthcare, and everything else each year?
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

Proposition 1
Should the state be authorized to issue $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to support building and preserving affordable housing, expanding homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income residents, veterans and homelessness programs?
The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 would authorize a general obligation bond, $10 billion of which would fund affordable housing and related infrastructure projects. Another $1.25 billion would fund the CalVet Home Loan Program. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) reports bond funds would support up to 40,000 rental units and could also assist 40,000 families in buying a home.
Yes Argument
Proposition 1 builds and preserves affordable homes and expands homeownership opportunities without raising taxes. It unlocks federal matching funds and fast-tracks construction. This measure will benefit veterans, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, at-risk foster youth, working families and people with disabilities.
No Argument
This package represents $11 billion in debt that taxpayers will add to their credit card with no reforms. We know the cost of building in California is exponentially higher than it needs to be. We have to reform that by first cutting costly regulations before we take out the credit card and borrow money.

No Argument

arguments.query: CalMatters Prop 1 2026 housing bond what to know

content.text:
1. Here's what to know about Prop 1, CA's $11 billion housing ... https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/ # There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the ballot this November. Here’s what you should know ... Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. ... For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws trying to address that by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quit 2. CA voter guide: Proposition 1, housing bond https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/ # Proposition 1 Borrow $11.25 billion for housing Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot. ... ## Summary ### Support California needs more money for housing in order to help the state’s more than 180,000 homeless residents, as well as those who pay more than they can afford in rent and those who can’t afford to purchase a home. ### Oppose Some Republican legislators criticized the bill for using veterans to drum up support while actually doing little to serve them. They also questioned the wisdom of borrowing more money to pay for housing without addressing the underlying reasons it’s so expensive to build. ... ## Ballot text **AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.** Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. **Fiscal Impact:** Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million ann 3. Why are there so many bonds on the California ballot? Here's what $44 billion would buy https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/ Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. ... Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 for housing and Proposition 38 for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. ... ## Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Re 4. Why are so many bonds on the California ballot? Proposition 1
Should the state be authorized to issue $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to support building and preserving affordable housing, expanding homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income residents, veterans and homelessness programs?
The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 would authorize a general obligation bond, $10 billion of which would fund affordable housing and related infrastructure projects. Another $1.25 billion would fund the CalVet Home Loan Program. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) reports bond funds would support up to 40,000 rental units and could also assist 40,000 families in buying a home.
Yes Argument
Proposition 1 builds and preserves affordable homes and expands homeownership opportunities without raising taxes. It unlocks federal matching funds and fast-tracks construction. This measure will benefit veterans, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, at-risk foster youth, working families and people with disabilities.
No Argument
This package represents $11 billion in debt that taxpayers will add to their credit card with no reforms. We know the cost of building in California is exponentially higher than it needs to be. We have to reform that by first cutting costly regulations before we take out the credit card and borrow money.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the ballot this November. Here’s what you should know

By Marisa Kendall, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 aims to address that crisis.

It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. 

A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.

Legislators have passed multiple laws trying to address that by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. 

A recent report estimated nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the ballot this November. Here’s what you should know

By Marisa Kendall, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 aims to address that crisis.

It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. 

A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.

Legislators have passed multiple laws trying to address that by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. 

A recent report estimated nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Photo by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo In summary Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. On November 3, 2026, California voters face a critical decision on Proposition 1, officially titled the Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure.
Passed by the state legislature via Senate Bill 417, Proposition 1 asks voters to authorize the state to issue $11.25 billion in General Obligation bonds.
The proposed allocation includes $10 billion for state-subsidized affordable housing programs, ranging from low-income multifamily construction and supportive housing to downpayment assistance and farmworker housing, alongside $1.25 billion designated for the CalVet Home Loan program.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO), repaying this debt will cost California taxpayers between $500 million and $600 million annually out of the General Fund for approximately 25 years, bringing the total long-term cost—including principal and accrued interest—to upwards of $13 billion to $15 billion (and potentially higher depending on prevailing interest rates).
For the California Moderate, a voter who identifies as both fiscally conservative and socially liberal, ballot measures like Proposition 1 present a classic policy dilemma.
Social liberals care deeply about human dignity, housing access, reducing homelessness, and aiding vulnerable populations.
Fiscal conservatives, on the other hand, demand prudent debt management, efficient allocation of public capital

Props. 1 and 38 would take the state deeper in debt for uncertain gains
Two measures on the November ballot ask voters to borrow $20 billion combined. Proposition 1 would fund housing programs. Proposition 38 would fund immunology research. We recommend a no vote on each.
The state already carries a heavy debt load. California owed about $70 billion on general obligation bonds as of Sept. 1, according to the state treasurer. Voters and lawmakers have authorized nearly $38 billion more in bonds that have not yet been sold.
The bondholders who lent the state money expect to be paid back with interest. The state spends about $6 billion annually from the general fund repaying bonds. Props. 1 and 38 would add roughly $1 billion to that for 20 to 25 years.
When state revenue comes up short, lawmakers can reduce spending or at least slow spending growth. Bond payments, however, are a legal obligation that comes due regardless. Every dollar locked into debt service is a taxpayer dollar unavailable for schools, health care or wildfire protection in a lean year.
Prop. 1: Housing money without accountability
California needs more housing, and Prop. 1 would throw $11.25 billion at the problem without addressing the underlying causes of the state’s housing shortage and high costs. Lawmakers took the easy route. Rather than pass controversial reforms or find money in the budget, they chose to ask voters to borrow.
Most of the money, about $7.2 billion, would pay for building, buying and rehabilitating multifamily rental housing, affordable housing and supportive housing for the homeless. Smaller pools of money totaling about $2.3 billion would provide mortgage and down-payment assistance.
Giving buyers more money with which to bid without adding homes would push prices higher. And buying existing apartments does not add a single home to ease market pressure.
The measure also lacks accountability. It calls for an annual report on how well things are going, but there is no independent audit on most of it and no remedy if the return on investment is lackluster. There also are no plans for when the money runs out and no guarantee that lawmakers will not meddle and reapportion the funds.
Californians have cause for skepticism that the state will spend this housing money well. A 2024 state audit found that California had not consistently tracked whether its homelessness spending worked. Sacramento should prove that it can measure and deliver results before asking for bonds that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
Prop. 38: Science by ballot box
Immunology and immunotherapy hold real promise, but Prop. 38 is the wrong way to fund research into them. Only one University of California-affiliated institute appears to qualify for half of the money, according to a CalMatters analysis. Coincidentally, that institute’s co-founder is one of Prop. 38’s biggest backers.
One problem with this approach is that state law would lock in how the money could be spent. Research dollars should support the centers with the most promising results and best scientists. Maybe that is the UC affiliate now, but that could change.
Bonds also fit research poorly. They are better suited to bridges and schools that last decades than to research that might never bear fruit. Even if there are commercial breakthroughs, the Legislative Analyst’s Office says royalties could take decades to repay the bonds, if they ever do.
Medical research is a legitimate state interest. If California wants to fund it, the state ought to do so through the regular budget process, weighing its value against other state priorities, not with a special bond that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
