Is the answer to California’s housing crisis more bonds and more debt? Of course not.
Yet that’s what’s being pitched with Proposition 1.
Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature via Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), Prop. 1 asks voters to approve (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) $11.25 billion in bonds to help finance various programs, including a $500 million down payment assistance program.
One bond – $1.25 billion – will go toward the Department of Veteran Affairs (CalVet) Home Loan Program. Participants in the program will repay this portion of Prop. 1.
The other $10 billion bond will be paid out of the state’s General Fund, and will go toward various programs. Most of it will go toward subsidized housing for low-income residents, while other funds will go toward programs aimed at student housing, tribes and farmworkers.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, Prop. 1 “would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students.”
Proponents say Prop. 1 is worth the cost given the state’s high rate of homelessness and the high proportion of renters who struggle with high housing costs. In backing the measure, California YIMBY argues that, “Publicly-funded housing subsidies for low-income Californians who cannot afford market-rate rents are a good thing, and they should be more widely available.”
Yeah, no.
Taxpayer-subsidized housing in California is incredibly expensive to build. As a RAND Corp. report (https://backtobasicssj.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/RAND_RRA3743-1.pdf) from last year points out, publicly-subsidized “affordable” housing in California costs 1.5 times that of market rate housing “and more than four times the cost of market-rate housing in Texas.”
There are myriad reasons for this, of course. As much progress as California has made in loosening zoning laws, the state’s land-use policies remain restrictive. Permitting processes in major cities are often incredibly slow (https://x.com/esoltas/status/2098162675989565925/photo/1) . Reprieves from the California Environmental Quality Act always come with costly strings attached, including labor mandates.
Throwing more money into housing that’s slow and expensive to build simply won’t accomplish very much, because it can’t.
California YIMBY, to its credit, also points out some of the less desirable features of the measure. The down payment assistance program, for example, might be nice for those who benefit from it, but given the low supply of housing, it could end up contributing to higher home prices.
Then there’s the total bill for all of this. The $10 billion general obligation bond will, after interest, cost far more than that and further crowd-out other spending in the state budget. According to the LAO, the state will be spending $500 million to $600 million a year for 25 years to pay off the bond.
This, in turn, will only put further pressure on the perpetually precarious state budget and increase the risk of the Legislature approving or seeking new and higher taxes. This is no idle threat considering state lawmakers contemplated hundreds of billions of dollars (https://www.caltax.org/foundation/reports/20260611_Tax_and_Fee_Report.pdf) in new taxes this legislative session.
Eight years ago, in opposing the very similar Proposition 1 in 2018, we wrote (https://www.ocregister.com/2018/09/18/proposition-1-is-not-the-answer-to-our-housing-crisis-vote-no/) , “If California’s leaders are serious about making California a more affordable place to live, they should concentrate their efforts on curtailing onerous regulations and restrictive land-use policies and making it easier for homebuilders to build. And if they insist on subsidizing housing, they should do so directly, rather than wasting taxpayer money on interest payments.”
We stand by that, though we’d emphasize the need for California to stop fiddling and burdening reforms with mandates. There are those who argue California can both subsidize housing and loosen regulations, but the reality that we’re still having this discussion underscores that state and local leaders are dragging their feet and not deregulating fast enough.
California needs more housing, yes, but it doesn’t need Prop. 1.
Prop. 1 squanders billions into expensive housing and other gimmicks to buy political support.
Vote no and demand better housing policies.

by Max Dubler
Introduction
The 2026 Affordable Housing Bond – Proposition 1
This fall, California voters will vote on an $11.25 billion bond measure, Proposition 1, to fund housing programs, including Affordable Housing construction. California YIMBY recommends a “yes” vote on Prop 1.
This analysis is intended to explain what Affordable Housing is, how Prop 1 dollars will be used, and what effect the measure will have.
Analysis
What Does “Affordable Housing” Mean And How Is It Different From Housing Affordability?
When most people talk about “affordable housing” in casual conversation, they are referring to market rate housing that fits within their personal budget or homes that middle class people can afford. That is not how policymakers use this phrase.
In housing policy conversations, “Affordable Housing” is a technical term that refers to price-regulated housing for people making specified incomes (more on this in a moment). Affordable Housing properties usually have a covenant written into the property’s deed that requires the homes to be rented at certain levels of affordability, which is why you’ll sometimes hear Affordable Housing referred to as “deed-restricted Affordable Housing.” Most of this type of “affordable housing” is subsidized by the government, using revenues from taxes and bonds.
“Housing affordability,” on the other hand, refers to the relationship between your income and your rent. If your total monthly housing cost is below 30% of your income, your housing is considered “affordable” to you. If it’s between 30 and 50% of your monthly income, you are “cost burdened.” If it’s over 50% of your monthly income, you are “severely cost burdened.”
Researchers and policymakers measure housing affordability by comparing median incomes to median rents and home prices.
Subsidized Housing
Most housing subsidy programs work by paying the difference between 30% of a tenant’s income and the actual cost (amortized construction, finance, and operations/maintenance costs) of their housing. There are two main ways of doing this: vouchers, which subsidize rents for tenants in privately-owned housing; and Affordable Housing, where the building itself is subsidized.
The Housing Choice Voucher program, commonly known as Section 8 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_8_(housing)), is the largest federal housing subsidy program, serving about 2.3 million households (California YIMBY supports fully funding Section 8 (https://cayimby.org/resources/policy-framework/chapter-2/#fund-section-8).).
Section 8 vouchers subsidize voucher holders’ rent by paying landlords the difference between 30% of the tenant’s income, and the market-rate rent for their home. Only 10% of eligible families receive Section 8 vouchers (https://www.cbpp.org/research/housing/families-wait-years-for-housing-vouchers-due-to-inadequate-funding), both because the program is under-funded, and because the general shortage of market-rate housing makes it hard for voucher holders to find vacant homes. Los Angeles last opened the voucher wait list in 2022 (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/section-8-housing-choice-voucher-los-angeles-city-applications-lottery-hacla-affordable-homelessness), when it got 223,000 applications for 30,000 spots on the list (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/section-8-housing-choice-voucher-los-angeles-city-applications-lottery-hacla-affordable-homelessness).
Subsidized affordable housing, on the other hand, provides a subsidy to the physical housing structure itself. Tenants in Affordable Housing pay rent based on their incomes. Rent is usually set at 30% of the upper income limit for the unit.
There are different levels of affordability in Affordable Housing, which are set according to the tenant’s family size and income as it relates to the county-level area median income (AMI):
Moderate Income 80-120% of AMI
Low Income – 50-80% of AMI
Very Low Income – 30-50% of AMI
Extremely Low Income 0-30% of AMI
Different housing subsidies define incomes and rents slightly differently. You can see the income limits (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/ctcac/2026%20Income%20Limits%205-1-26%2B%20-%20ADA_0.pdf) and rent levels (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/ctcac/2026%20Rent%20Limits%205-1-26%2B%20-%20ADA_0.pdf) for various state and federal programs in California here (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/income-limits/state-federal-income-limits). Also, while there is some Affordable Housing for ownership, like Habitat for Humanity houses, most Affordable Housing is for rent.
Because rents are set at 30% of the upper limit of monthly incomes for the unit, many Affordable Housing tenants spend more than 30% of their incomes on rent, making them rent burdened.
The Vast Majority Of Low-Income Californians Do Not Live In Affordable Housing
84% of California’s lower-income households (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CHP_Unsubsidized-At-Risk-2026-FINAL_.pdf) live in unsubsidized, market-rate housing, not income-restricted Affordable Housing. There are about 600,000 total subsidized Affordable Housing units (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CHP_Subsidized-At-Risk-2026-FINAL.pdf) in California, making up about 4% of the state’s 14,880,000 total homes (https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT1Y2024.B25002?g=040XX00US06).
California YIMBY believes that we should help these low-income renters by increasing the supply of housing across the board to chip away at the housing shortage, which is the primary cause of unaffordable rents.
The Finance Gap, Or Why Affordable Housing Requires Funding
Before a new apartment is built, its investors and financers use a projection of rents and operating incomes to ensure the project will not lose money over the expected life of the building. Most of the time, the construction and development costs are paid off by a building’s rental income over the first 20 to 30 years of its life, after which rents cover ongoing maintenance and necessary upgrades.
However, lower-income tenants often cannot afford rents that are high enough to pay off the cost of building new homes. This creates a “financing gap” for people who want brand new apartments to be affordable to low-income tenants: someone has to pay the difference between the rents that these tenants can afford and the actual cost of building and maintaining homes for them.
There are two main ways of closing this gap: publicly-funded housing subsidies, and unfunded affordability mandates in new housing projects, which are often referred to as “inclusionary zoning” (IZ) requirements.
Unfunded Affordability Mandates Are Bad Policy (https://cayimby.org/resources/policy-framework/chapter-1/#subsidized-affordability) That Worsen The Housing Shortage
The stated intentions behind most inclusionary zoning (IZ) — the practice of requiring developers to offer a percentage of new housing units at below-market rents — are good. But cities routinely set the affordability requirements so high that building becomes financially infeasible (https://www.spur.org/news/2026-06-25/realigning-housing-policy-real-world-economics-san-francisco).
IZ mandates, unless accompanied by external subsidies, rely entirely on market rents to cross-subsidize affordable units, which homebuilders rent at a loss. This cross-subsidy only works if the market rents are high enough to produce the necessary surplus. In other words, IZ mandates are only workable when market rents far exceed the cost of construction, which only happens under conditions of housing scarcity.
In cases where market rents aren’t high enough to allow for cross-subsidization, landowners will usually opt out of building multifamily housing. Perversely, this meansIZ can actually exacerbate an area’s housing shortage (https://cayimby.org/blog/getting-by-on-reduced-supply-the-impact-of-affordability-mandates/) and lead to more displacement.
In fact, the very logic of IZ is flawed. The construction of more housing, including more market-rate housing, benefits the public by creating vacancies (https://cayimby.org/blog/movin-on-up-how-costly-new-homes-create-affordable-old-homes/) in the cheapest homes (https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/03/18/austins-surge-of-new-housing-construction-drove-down-rents). But IZ is premised on the notion that developers reap all the benefits from building new housing, and that the public needs a mechanism for extracting some benefit of its own. In the process, IZ ends up needlessly discouraging (https://cayimby.org/blog/the-tradeoffs-of-inclusionary-zoning-a-closer-look/) the production of a good that California needs more of. Further, IZ places the entire financial burden of funding subsidized housing on renters who live in multifamily housing while letting the truly wealthy — who overwhelmingly live in single-family homes they own — off the hook. (One analysis (https://cayimby.org/blog/california-cities-wanted-free-affordable-housing-turns-out-theres-a-huge-cost/) found that each inclusionary unit costs renters $800,000 in excess rent.)
Instead of requiring market rate renters to bear the cost of housing subsidies, the state should subsidize affordable housing itself.
This brings us to the Affordable Housing bond, which would provide significant funding for subsidized housing.
What Will This Bond Do?
If voters approve the bond, the state of California will issue $11.25 billion in general obligation debt, to be repaid from existing state tax receipts, and use the revenues to fund the following:
New Construction ($8.05 billion)
$5.1 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp), the main state fund for building Affordable apartment complexes.
$1.15 billion to supportive housing administered through the MHP program. “Supportive housing” is Affordable Housing with on-site social services, usually reserved for people leaving homelessness.
$600 million to the CalHOME Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/calhome), which supports for-sale Affordable Housing, often built by Habitat for Humanity.
$450 million to the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/fwhg).
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/tribes/thgp) for tribal housing.
$350 million for student housing, divided between the UC and CSU systems.
$200 million for an Affordable Housing Innovation Fund to support local pilot programs.
Acquiring, Upgrading, and Recapitalizing Existing Housing ($950 million)
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/prp), which renovates and re-capitalizes existing Affordable Housing.
$200 million for a program to be created by the Legislature that will buy existing market rate housing and convert it to Affordable Housing.
Other Purposes ($2.25 billion)
$500 million for the Home Purchase Assistance Fund to provide down payment assistance.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/iig), which funds things like sewer upgrades, street improvements, and site preparation necessary to facilitate affordable and mixed-income infill housing.
$1.25 billion for home loans for veterans.
So what will all this money do in practice?
The Infill Infrastructure Grant Program Is Good
Established in 2019, the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program provides state gap funding for capital improvement projects like sewer upgrades, street improvements, and site preparation necessary to facilitate affordable and mixed-income infill housing. Its purpose is to facilitate infill housing construction, and funding it is a good use of public money.
This brings us to the new construction funding, which is the bulk of the bond.
This Bond Will Build About 43,700 Affordable Homes
How many homes will this bond build? Affordable Housing developers expect to take the $8 billion in bond funding and leverage it to get about four times as much money from the federal government using the Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), a major source of Affordable Housing funding. A UC Berkeley analysis of Affordable Housing construction costs in California (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Low-Income-Housing-Tax-Credit-Construction-Costs-An-Analysis-of-Prevailing-Wages-August-2024.pdf) found that “in 2023, it cost approximately $708,000 to develop one [new construction] subsidized housing unit funded with Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity in California.” If we are able to secure federal funds and build at 2023’s development cost, the production funding in bond will produce about 57,000 new Affordable Homes for low-income Californians.
Given the increase in construction and interest costs since 2023, the Legislative Analyst’s Office estimate (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) that “the bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students” seems accurate.
$500 Million In Down Payment Assistance Could Drive Up Home Prices
California housing is expensive because there are not enough homes to accommodate everyone who wants to live here. Allocating $500 million for down payment assistance to help homebuyers buy existing homes on the open market will increase demand.
Absent new supply, this could increase competition for scarce housing and drive up home prices. The buyers who get the assistance will win, at the cost of driving up prices overall.
Investing $950 Million In Existing Housing Is Good, But Won’t Reduce Rents
Building lots of new homes is the only way to durably reduce housing costs across the board in high-demand regions like California.
Spending $950 million to rehabilitate existing Affordable Housing, and buy existing market rate housing and restrict the rents, will help the current and future residents of those buildings. But these funds will not expand the housing supply, and so will not bring down rents.
Pro-Housing Voters Should Vote Yes
Publicly-funded housing subsidies for low-income Californians who cannot afford market-rate rents are a good thing, and they should be more widely available (https://cayimby.org/resources/policy-framework/chapter-2#fund-section-8). Many of the programs this grant will fund are excellent. Pro-housing voters should vote YES on Prop 1.
To make sure we get as much value from this investment as possible, the state legislature should reduce the complexity of securing funding (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/blog/reducing-the-complexity-in-californias-affordable-housing-finance-system/) by offering true “one stop shop” financing for qualifying projects, create streamlined entitlement and permitting processes that do not impose additional costs, and use some of the Affordable Housing Innovation Fund money to fund the Affordable Housing portion of large projects subject to Inclusionary Zoning.
Policymakers should also follow the overwhelming evidence (https://www.buildingabundance.ca/p/vacancy-chains) that new market rate housing induces a “moving on up” effect that particularly benefits tenants in inexpensive older buildings (https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/03/18/austins-surge-of-new-housing-construction-drove-down-rents), and enact broad zoning and permitting reforms that will allow limited subsidy dollars to go further and help more tenants (https://cayimby.org/blog/how-a-boom-in-market-rate-housing-would-help-section-8-tenants/).
Further, the Affordable Housing industry should stop lobbying against (https://www.insidephilanthropy.com/home/philanthropy-needs-to-pick-a-side-on-the-housing-construction-debate) common-sense zoning and permitting reforms (https://cal.streetsblog.org/2021/05/19/parking-requirements-are-not-a-useful-bargaining-chip-for-increasing-affordable-housing) that will reduce housing costs by expanding the supply of new unsubsidized homes for middle-class families at no cost to taxpayers.
Further Reading

Nearly 40,000 affordable homes that could serve more than 432,000 low-income households over the next 55 years are awaiting final funding to begin construction in California, according to Enterprise research.
While the 2026 California Affordable Housing Pipeline shows strong development momentum, the analysis makes clear that without adequate public funding, these shovel-ready projects will not move forward.

- Invest urgent state funding through the 2026-27 budget
- Pass the 2026 Affordable Housing Bond Act and pave the way for permanent funding
- Streamline the housing finance system and improve cost-efficiency
- Confront operational challenges.

I have a clear enough picture of the debate, so next I'm weighing whether subsidized affordable housing adds net supply or crowds out private construction, since that decides whether it actually helps broader affordability. I'm going to look for the evidence on crowd-out, starting with the studies I recall, such as Eriksen & Rosenthal (2010) and Baum-Snow & Marion (2009).

I'm weighing the case that in tightly regulated markets, subsidized housing might add real net supply by getting around zoning through density bonuses, which cuts against the older crowd-out findings. I want to check whether any recent California-specific work backs that up. I'm also thinking about whether bond financing suits housing, given how long these assets last, and how the roughly $500–600M a year would compare against a General Fund with large structural deficits. Then there's the question of whether vouchers would stretch the money further than project-based construction.

I'm checking the accountability side next: the program only gets an annual report with no independent audit, and the legislature can move funds between programs. Then I'm working through the costs, which look like roughly $17B over 30 years once interest is included, with a per-unit state subsidy in the range of $180K. Before I settle on a view, I'm also weighing whether giving a personal recommendation on a ballot measure is something I should do.

I'm weighing whether to give a personal yes or no on this housing bond, since it's a contested policy call where editorial boards and reasonable people split on the values and the cost-effectiveness. I'm inclined to lean toward laying out the strongest case on each side rather than picking one, because a ballot choice like this is mainly the voter's to make.

I'm going to frame this as a values-and-evidence choice rather than give a verdict, since it's a contested ballot call. I'm settling on not giving a yes or no on this ballot measure, since it's a values-and-evidence call that voters should make for themselves. I'd rather be clear about why than just decline, so I'm planning to explain the tradeoff and what would tip it either way.

Nonpartisan outlets and analysts like LAO and PPIC generally avoid recommending votes, which points toward staying even-handed here.

I'm settling on the view that the vote is genuinely contested, with no empirical consensus and a values split that runs along party lines, so I shouldn't hand over a personal yes or no. Proposition
1 $11.25 billion bond for affordable and veterans housing
Our read Toss-up: real backlog, no cost fix
$11.25B builds subsidized units at about $630K each through an agency that has ignored audit fixes since 2018. The backlog is real; the cost problem isn’t addressed.
Share Copy for AI
Markdown (https://www.californiapeople.org/md/prop-1.md)Use with AI agents (https://www.californiapeople.org/ai.html)
Type Legislative bond act (SB 417, Limón)
Sponsor Legislature; campaign funded by affordable-housing developers and their allies
Campaign money
$15.3M yes $0 no
Your pick
# Key findings
A subsidized apartment built with California tax credits cost about $630,000 per unit in 2023, up nearly 20% since 2019 after inflation. [1]
The state's share in this bond works out to roughly $180,000 per rental unit ($7.2B for up to 40,000 units, our math). The rest has to come from tax credits and local money. [2]
RAND estimates that at Colorado's cost levels, about $1.25B of recent spending by California's four biggest housing programs would have built more than 4 times as many units . [3]
The State Auditor has flagged the agency that runs these bonds (HCD) in five audits (2007–2018) : weak monitoring, unexplained high per-unit costs, and a data system that never worked fully. [4] [5] [6]
The campaign is funded mostly by the groups that would apply for the money: $13.9M of $15.3M came from a committee sponsored by affordable-housing organizations. [7]
The split you vote on isn't fixed. The bond act lets the Legislature "amend this chapter in order to reallocate the proceeds" among its programs by ordinary statute, with no further vote of the people. [8]
# Track record
Bond
State $
What it produced (as reported)
Notes
Prop 46 (2002)
$2.1B
~91,000 "units assisted" for $1.91B awarded
Count includes 10,000+ shelter and dorm spaces, so it isn't a count of new apartments. [9]
Prop 1C (2006)
$2.85B
~114,000 "units assisted" for ~$2.3B
Includes ~3,000 shelter spaces. HCD's own report gives two different dollar totals. [9]
Prop 1 (2018)
$4B ($3B housing + $1B veteran loans)
LAO estimated subsidies for up to 30,000 multifamily and 7,500 farmworker households. We found no HCD count of completed units
Money ran out quickly amid heavy demand; HCD expected to use it all by end of 2024. [10] [11] [12]
Prop 1 (Mar 2024)
$6.38B ($2B housing)
Estimated up to 4,350 units
Behavioral-health bond. Passed with 50.2%. [13] [7]
Prop 1 (2026)
$11.25B
LAO: up to 40,000 rentals + ~40,000 homebuyer households
Nearly 3 times the size of the 2018 bond. [14]
Audit pattern: In 2014 the State Auditor found that 7 of 10 sampled projects cost well above local averages with no documented justification. One project (East Leland Family Apartments) cost ~$412,000 per unit when comparable projects averaged ~$264,000. The auditor also found a $1.35M grant for an outdoor "green living room" that built no housing, $486M still waiting to be awarded, and HCD's cost benchmarks hadn't been updated since 2008. [4]
# Money and conflicts
Yes $15.3M, No $0 in committees (through Oct 22). [7] Reform California has spent about $7,500 against. [12] Top Yes donors include Airbnb, two carpenters' union councils, and Building a Better California (funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr), at $1M each. [14]
Recipients are mostly nonprofit and for-profit affordable-housing developers, who apply to HCD and CalHFA. For example, MidPen Housing alone has 1,198 units waiting on state money. [15]
Supporters cite 461 "shovel-ready" projects (39,880 units) stalled for lack of gap funding. That count comes from Enterprise Community Partners, an affordable-housing finance group. [15]
# Does it solve a lasting problem?
It adds units, but it doesn't touch the cost per unit, which is the main reason each dollar builds so little. Every extra funding source a project needs adds about 4 months and ~$20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The state needs about 1 million lower-income units by 2030 under its own targets. This bond covers roughly 4% of that. [15] [2]
Our read is a toss-up. The backlog of ready projects is real and no one is organized against the bond. But the evidence on this page runs one way: cost per unit is the problem, the bond doesn't touch it, the agency has left the 2018 audit fixes untouched, and the campaign is funded by the applicants. Vote yes if you weigh the backlog more; vote no if you want the cost problem fixed first.
# If you vote yes: accountability
Bottom line: Most of the $10B goes out as competitive awards from one department (HCD) with no cost-per-unit limit in the law. The bill only requires an annual report (§ 54088), and it lets agencies write the program rules without the usual public rulemaking (§ 54077). [8] Watching how the money is spent is up to voters, reporters and the Legislature.
# Who spends it, and who answers for it
Money
Run by
Who's accountable
$7.2B rentals, $600M CalHome, $500M infill infrastructure, $450M farmworker, $200M tribal, $200M local pilots
HCD
HCD Director Gustavo Velasquez (since 2020) [18] ; Secretary Tomiquia Moss of the new California Housing and Homelessness Agency (since June 2026) [19] ; the Governor, who appoints both
$500M down-payment help
CalHFA
Executive Director Tony Sertich [20]
$350M student housing
UC and CSU
UC Regents and CSU Trustees
$1.25B veterans' home loans
CalVet
An independent accountant must review the loan program every year while the bonds are outstanding. [8]
The tax credits most rentals also need
Tax Credit Allocation Committee (CTCAC)
Chaired by the State Treasurer. Other voting members: the Controller, the Finance Director, and the heads of HCD and CalHFA. [20] The Treasurer and Controller races are both on this ballot.
# Who gets the money
Applicants are nonprofit and for-profit developers, cities, counties and tribes. From 2019 to 2025, HCD funded 66,511 rental units . Of those, 26,904 (40%) are listed as completed so far , and 14,660 hadn't started construction. Projects funded in the last two or three years can't be finished yet, so the number to watch is whether the older awards close out. [21]
No single public database lists each HCD award with its developer, cost per unit and status. HCD's summary gives counts only. The best project-level records are CTCAC's staff reports, which list each tax-credit project's developer, units and total cost. [22]
# Red flags already on record
Fraud charges: Shangri-La Industries won about $115M in state Homekey contracts for about 500 homes. Its $27M Thousand Oaks project sits abandoned. Its former CFO was federally charged with mail fraud in Oct 2025 and has pleaded not guilty. [23] [17] The state, through Attorney General Bonta, sued the company in Jan 2024, alleging breach of contract and fraud. [24]
Close to home: San Bernardino's All Star Lodge, a Homekey motel conversion, was foreclosed after two years. No affordability restriction had been recorded, so the new owner could threaten big rent increases. [17] [25]
Homekey's record: $3.8B awarded since 2020. About 1 in 5 promised homes were unfinished at the end of 2024, and at least 10 awards (about 500 units) were canceled or clawed back. No state agency has publicly analyzed the program in detail. [17] This matters here because Prop 1's $1.15B supportive-housing share can fund the same kind of interim-to-permanent conversions. [8]
Audit advice ignored: In 2018 the State Auditor told the Legislature to require HCD to report every year on how it monitors bond programs, and to have its parent agency track HCD's progress. As of Jan 2026, the status of both is "No action taken." The audit's recommendations on HCD's administrative-cost overspending are still listed as only partially implemented or pending. [6]
Money lost, units unclear: A state committee let about $2.7B in housing bond authority expire in 2015–2017 without saying so publicly. The housing agencies don't share a project ID, so their unit counts may overlap. [26]
Evaluation blocked: AB 505 would have had the LAO evaluate Homekey. It died in the Assembly Housing Committee in Jan 2026 without a hearing. [27]
Not on the high-risk list: The State Auditor's Dec 2025 high-risk list doesn't include housing or homelessness spending. [28]
# Who to press, and what to ask for
Your Assemblymember and state Senator (look them up at findyourrep.legislature.ca.gov). Ask them to:
Pass the 2018 audit recommendation into law: public, project-by-project reporting for every Prop 1 award (developer, units, cost per unit, start and completion dates).
Ask the Joint Legislative Audit Committee to have the State Auditor audit the first round of Prop 1 awards. Any legislator can request an audit.
Bring back the Homekey evaluation that AB 505 proposed.
Lower the cost per unit: fund each project from fewer sources, since each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit [1] [15] , and adopt RAND's recommendations: a 30-day approval deadline, synchronized inspections, lower impact fees ($29,000 per unit in California vs. $12,000 in Colorado), and fewer design rules that don't affect safety. [3]
Treasurer and Controller candidates: they'll sit on CTCAC. Ask whether they'll score tax-credit applications on cost per unit and publish final costs for every finished project.
CTCAC and HCD meetings take public comment. Agendas are posted on the Treasurer's and HCD's websites.
Report waste or fraud to the State Auditor's whistleblower hotline: auditor.ca.gov/hotline or 800-952-5665. You can file anonymously. [29]
# Public records to request (CPRA)
The California Public Records Act is the state's version of FOIA. Anyone can file a request, and you don't need to give a reason. The agency must respond within 10 days, or within 24 days in unusual cases. [30] Send HCD requests through its online portal or to PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov (mailto:PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov). [31]
To HCD: Under the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code § 7920.000 et seq.), I request records sufficient to show, for every award made from Proposition 1 (2018) and Proposition 1 (2024) bond funds: project name, sponsor and developer, city, award amount and date, number of units, total development cost, and current status (not started, under construction, or completed, with the completion date). I also request any notices of default, recapture or cancellation for these awards. I prefer electronic records in their original format, such as a spreadsheet. Please state the estimated date the records will be available, as Gov. Code § 7922.535 requires.
To HCD: All monitoring reports, notices of default, and recapture or settlement records for Homekey projects sponsored by Shangri-La Industries, and for the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino.
To CTCAC (State Treasurer's Office): For every tax-credit project in San Bernardino County awarded from 2019 to 2025, the final cost certification showing the total development cost at completion, alongside the cost in the application.
What it does
$10B of the general-obligation bonds, repaid from the General Fund: $7.2B affordable rentals, $1.1B homeownership, $500M infrastructure, $450M farmworker housing, $350M UC/CSU student housing, $200M tribal housing, $200M local pilots. [2]
$1.25B CalVet home loans, repaid by veterans' loan payments (the program "has always operated at no direct cost to the state"). [2]
Cost: $500–600M a year for about 25 years. [2]
What we're not asking
Each bond is bigger and buys less. State housing bonds went $2.1B (2002), $2.85B (2006), $4B (2018), $11.25B (2026), while the cost of a tax-credit unit rose nearly 20% after inflation from 2019 to 2023. [9] [2] [1] Play it forward: a yes vote with no cost reform sets up a larger ask around 2030.
Subsidy chases a fixed pipeline. Most of these projects also need federal tax credits, which are capped. More state gap money doesn't add credits; it funds the same projects with one more layer, and each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The debt stacks. The state had $70.7B in general-obligation bonds outstanding and $39.9B authorized but unsold as of March 2026. Prop 1 adds $10B and Prop 38 another $8.4B, each costing $500–600M a year from the same General Fund that pays for schools and Medi-Cal. [16] [2]
Who checks year 30? Affordability covenants run for decades, but at the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino no covenant was even recorded. Nobody is funded to monitor covenants over the life of the bond. [17]
Game theory. Developers fund the campaign, win the awards, and fund the next bond. The Legislature can shift the split later by statute. HCD has no reason to fix its data when the money comes anyway. The bond vote is the only lever voters hold.
Better or worse in 20 years? Roughly 40,000 households housed, which is real. The cost structure, the data gap and the debt all stay. More units, same machine.
Open questions: Why does the bill cap nothing per unit? Where is the completed-unit count for the 2018 bond? Would a smaller bond tied to a cost cap have passed the Legislature?
Both sides
For: a real backlog of ready projects; rents are crushing low-income households; the bond funds farmworker, tribal and student housing that the market won't build.
Against: No official ballot argument against was filed. [32] Republican lawmakers, including Asm. Carl DeMaio, say only ~11% goes to veterans despite the name [12] , and that it borrows without addressing why building here costs so much [17] [33] ; RAND finds that at Colorado's costs, the same money would build 4x+ as many units. [3]

content.text:
I know you asked for just yes or no, but I'm not going to pick for you on a ballot measure. After reading the bill, the Legislative Analyst's report and the arguments on both sides, I don't think the facts settle it. It comes down to how much you weigh housing help against caution about debt and cost, and informed people disagree. California's major newspapers split too. Here's a quick way to decide.

**Vote YES if you mostly agree that:**
- The state should pay to build homes for low-income and homeless Californians, because private builders won't build them at rents those people can afford.
- It's better to fund about 40,000 approved affordable units that are stalled for lack of money now than to wait for reforms that lower building costs.
- About $500–600M a year (roughly 0.25% of the state budget) is a fair price for buildings that must stay affordable for 55 years.

**Vote NO if you mostly agree that:**
- California shouldn't take on new long-term debt when it expects budget deficits of $20–35B a year.
- At $600,000–700,000+ per subsidized unit, adding money without fixing costs is poor value.
- The state can't be trusted to spend this well without stronger oversight.

**What it does**
- It borrows $11.25B:
  - $10B is paid back from the state budget.
  - $1.25B funds home loans for veterans, which veterans repay through their mortgages. So despite the name, only about 11% is for veterans, and that part pays for itself.
- About $7.2B goes to building and renovating apartments with income limits. The rest pays for help with down payments, housing for farmworkers, tribes and students, and related infrastructure.
- Repayment runs $500–600M a year for about 25 years, roughly $13–17B in total.
- The Legislative Analyst estimates up to 40,000 rental units, plus homebuying help for up to 40,000 households.

**Best case for yes**
- **The backlog is real.** The money from the 2018 housing bond was all committed by 2023. The main state housing program gets about $9 in requests for every $1 it has.
- **Each dollar goes further.** Housing groups say each state dollar brings in about $4 from federal, local and private sources. The units stay affordable long after the bond is paid off.
- **The state can afford it.** Debt payments are about 3% of state revenue, below the historical average of about 4%.

**Best case for no**
- **It's poor value.** RAND, a research group, found subsidized housing in California costs 1.5× as much per square foot as regular new housing, and the bond sets no cost limits.
- **It won't lower prices for most people.** 40,000 units is about 4% of the state's need for lower-income housing. Research also finds subsidized buildings partly replace private ones that would have been built anyway. CA YIMBY supports the bond but warns the $500M in down-payment help could push home prices up.
- **Oversight is weak.** The bill mainly requires an annual report, and the Legislature can move money between programs without another public vote. The State Auditor's 2018 recommendations for tighter oversight of the housing department are still listed as "no action taken."

**Who's on each side**
- **Yes:** Gov. Newsom, the state Democratic Party, the CA Chamber of Commerce, CA YIMBY, SPUR, the League of Women Voters, labor unions, big-city mayors from both parties, the SF Chronicle and the Sacramento Bee.
- **No:** Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the California Taxpayers Association, the Libertarian Party, some Republican legislators, and the editorial boards of the Mercury News, OC Register, San Diego Union-Tribune and Press Democrat.
- The state Republican Party is neutral, and no one is funding a "no" campaign.

If you tell me which of these matters most to you, I'll turn it into a straight yes or no.
